# Volume 5 — CHAPTER XXI. THE IMPOSSIBLE WORD

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

John Ashdown ambled lost in thought amidst the sharp, fresh air of a winter evening in Fern Hollow. Past the town, the hills sparkled with the cold, magnificent radiance of snow under the moon. Along the sprawling valley, each tiny fir tree chanted a unique, untamed melody to the music of frost and wind. Down the eastern incline and gliding across the ice-covered pond, his children alongside the Carrow boys and girls were sledding. A wonderful time was being had by them, and their cheerful shouts and even happier laughter rang throughout the valley, fading into tiny, magical tones among the timber. To the right, through the grove of maples, the lights of Hollowmere shone with the warm, welcoming attraction that continuously appears to shine from the lamps of a dwelling where one understands love, gladness, and a reception exist for every relative, whether related by blood or soul. Now and then, Mr. Ashdown greatly enjoyed passing an evening debating with the doctor beside the driftwood fire, where the renowned china dogs of Hollowmere maintained an eternal guard, just as hearth gods ought to do, yet he did not glance in that direction this evening. Far away on the western hill, a dimmer but more captivating light shone. Mr. Ashdown was traveling to visit Clementine Ainslie, and he intended to reveal a matter to her that had been gradually developing inside his heart ever since they initially met and had bloomed completely on the night Grace had so enthusiastically expressed her praise for Clementine.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0000 }

He had come to understand that he had grown fond of Clementine. Naturally, it was not like his feelings for Cecilia. That was a totally distinct matter. He believed that particular love, filled with romance, dreams, and glamour, could never come back. Nevertheless, Clementine was lovely, sweet, and cherished—extremely cherished. A better companion could not be found. In her presence, he experienced more happiness than he had ever anticipated feeling again. For his house, she would make a perfect mistress, and for his children, a fine mother.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0001 }

In the time following the death of his wife, Mr. Ashdown had been given countless suggestions—coming from fellow Presbytery members, from various church members who were above suspicion of self-interest, and from a few who were not—that taking a second wife was something he should do: However, such suggestions failed to leave an impact on him. The general consensus was that he failed to notice them. Yet his awareness of them was actually very sharp. Moreover, during those moments when common sense briefly struck him, he recognized that finding a wife was indeed the practical course of action. Nevertheless, practical judgment was not a prominent trait in John Ashdown, and selecting a "suitable" female in a calculated, unemotional manner—much like hiring a housekeeper or taking on a business partner—represented a task he was entirely unable to perform. He despised the term "suitable" immensely. It brought James Perry to his mind with great intensity. “A suit able woman of suit able age,” that overly smooth fellow clergyman had remarked when dropping his exceedingly blatant suggestion. At that instant, John Ashdown experienced a truly astonishing urge to bolt wildly off and offer his hand in marriage to the most youthful, improper female he could possibly find.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0002 }

His good friend Mrs. Ambrose Kerr was liked by him. However, his feeling when she had directly informed him that he ought to remarry was like she had ripped off the curtain suspended in front of a holy altar of his deepest existence, and from that point onward he had been somewhat fearful of her. The existence of women “of suitable age” within his flock who would willingly wed him was known to him. Very early during his pastorate at Glen St. Agnes, that truth had penetrated through his complete detachment. Good, solid, tedious women they were, with a couple being reasonably attractive and the rest not quite that, and John Ashdown would have considered hanging himself just as willingly as wedding any single one of them. Unfaithful to certain ideals he possessed no apparent requirement could render him. No woman could be requested by him to take Cecilia’s spot within his house except if he was able to present her with a minimum portion of the devotion and reverence he had bestowed upon his young wife. Furthermore, where could such a female be located among the small number of women he knew?
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0003 }

Clementine Ainslie entered his existence on that evening in autumn, bearing a presence where his soul identified its true element. They joined hands in fellowship over the abyss of unfamiliarity. Within those ten minutes beside the concealed spring, he understood her more deeply than he understood Emmeline Drew or Elizabeth Kirk or Amy Annetta Fairlie over the course of a year, or ever could comprehend them throughout a hundred years. He had sought refuge with her for solace after Mrs. Hector Twiss offended his intellect and spirit, and he had received that comfort. From that moment forward, he frequently visited the dwelling atop the hill, moving along the darkened trails of evening in Fern Hollow with such skill that the chatter of the Glen was never able to confirm beyond doubt that his visits were to Clementine Ainslie. He had been discovered once or twice in the West living room by different guests; that comprised the sole evidence the Ladies’ Aid possessed. However, upon Elizabeth Kirk learning this, she discarded a quiet expectation she had permitted herself to hold, showing no transformation of look on her gentle, unpretentious visage, while Emmeline Drew decided that on her following encounter with a particular elderly unmarried man from Kettlebridge, she would refrain from dismissing him as she had during an earlier encounter. Naturally, should Clementine Ainslie set out to capture the clergyman, she was bound to capture him; her appearance seemed youthful for her age and gentlemen considered her attractive; furthermore, the Ainslie daughters possessed wealth!
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0004 }

“May he not prove so distracted that he accidentally asks Harriet to marry him,” represented the sole spiteful remark she permitted herself to utter to a compassionate sister Drew. Emmeline harbored no additional resentment toward Clementine. Ultimately, a single man without obligations was vastly superior to a widower possessing four offspring. It was merely the allure of the parsonage that had briefly obscured Emmeline’s vision regarding the superior choice.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0005 }

Passing Mr. Ashdown, a sled carrying three yelling riders hurtled toward the pond. Grace’s hair was flowing in the breeze, her long curls trailing, and the sound of her laughing rose above the rest. John Ashdown watched the trio go with a kind, wistful expression. It pleased him that his youngsters were companions with the Carrows—he was pleased they possessed a confidante as intelligent, cheerful, and gentle as Mrs. Carrow. Yet they lacked a further element, one that would be provided once he brought Clementine Ainslie to the old manse to be his wife. Possessed by her was a nature fundamentally motherly.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0006 }

Because it was Saturday evening, he rarely paid visits at that time, as those hours were meant for carefully reviewing his sermon for Sunday. Nevertheless, he had selected this particular evening after discovering that Harriet Ainslie would be out of town and Clementine would be by herself. Although he had frequently enjoyed agreeable evenings in the house on the hill, he had not, from the time of their initial encounter at the spring, ever found Clementine by herself. Harriet had invariably been present.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0007 }

It was not that he genuinely disapproved of Harriet’s presence. His fondness for Harriet Ainslie was great, and their friendship was of the highest order. Harriet possessed a mind that was nearly masculine, alongside a sense of humour that accorded exceptionally well with his own reserved, concealed enjoyment of wit. Her engagement with politics and global affairs pleased him. Within the Glen, including Dr. Carrow, no man possessed a superior comprehension of these matters.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0008 }

“I consider it just as good to maintain an interest in matters for the duration of your life,” she had stated. “If you fail to do so, it appears to me that little distinguishes the living from the deceased.”
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0009 }

His fondness extended to her agreeable, low, resonant voice, as well as the robust laughter that invariably concluded her cheerful, expertly narrated tales. Unlike the remaining females of Glen, she refrained from making sharp remarks concerning his offspring; she refrained from wearying him with neighborhood rumors; she possessed neither ill will nor small-mindedness. Her truthfulness was consistently grand. Adopting Miss Winifred’s method of categorizing individuals, Mr. Ashdown felt that Harriet was part of Joseph’s line. On the whole, she was an excellent person to have as a sister-in-law. Even so, a gentleman wished for the absence of even the finest females while he was offering marriage to a different lady. Yet Harriet remained constantly present. She refrained from demanding that Mr. Ashdown converse solely with her throughout the time. She allowed Clementine an equal portion of his attention. In fact, on numerous nights, Harriet withdrew almost completely, resting in the corner with St. Laurence held in her lap, while Mr. Ashdown and Clementine engaged in conversation, music, and joint reading. Occasionally, her existence slipped their minds entirely. Should their dialogue or duet selections display the slightest inclination toward what Harriet deemed flirty behavior, however, Harriet immediately crushed that inclination and sidelined Clementine for what remained of the night. Even the most stern among friendly guardians, however, cannot fully obstruct a particular delicate communication of glances, grins, and meaningful hushes; thus, the clergyman’s romantic pursuit advanced to a degree.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0010 }

However, if a peak were ever to be attained, that peak had to occur during Harriet’s absence. And Harriet was rarely absent, particularly during the winter months. She declared that she considered her own hearth to be the most delightful spot on earth. Traveling about possessed no charm for her. She enjoyed society, yet she desired to have it in her own house. Mr. Ashdown had nearly reached the point of believing he would have to express his thoughts to Clementine in a letter, when Harriet nonchalantly mentioned one night that she intended to attend a silver wedding the following Saturday evening. She had served as a bridesmaid at the original wedding of the couple. Because the invitation was restricted to old guests, Clementine was not among those invited. Mr. Ashdown listened with somewhat heightened interest, and a spark shone in his dark, dreamlike eyes. Harriet and Clementine both observed this; and Harriet and Clementine each experienced, with a sharp thrill, the realization that Mr. Ashdown was sure to ascend the hill the coming Saturday night.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0011 }

“We might just as well get this over with, St. Laurence,” Harriet firmly remarked to the black cat, once Mr. Ashdown had departed for home and Clementine had quietly headed upstairs. “He intends to propose to her, St. Laurence—I am completely certain of it. Therefore he ought to be given his opportunity to ask and discover that she is beyond his reach, Laurence. She would quite enjoy accepting him, Saint. I am aware of that—nevertheless she gave her word, and she must adhere to her word. I feel somewhat regretful in certain respects, St. Laurence. I am unaware of any man I would prefer more as a brother-in-law if having a brother-in-law were suitable. I have no objections to him, Saint—not a single objection other than his inability to recognize and be convinced that the Kaiser poses a threat to the peace of Europe. That constitutes his blind spot. Even so, he provides good companionship and I am fond of him. A female is able to speak whatever she desires to a male possessing a mouth such as John Ashdown’s and remain confident she will not be misconstrued. A gentleman of that sort is worth more than rubies, Saint—and far less common, Laurence. Even so, Clementine is not for him—and I imagine that once he learns she is unavailable to him he will abandon the two of us. And we will long for his presence, Saint—we will long for his presence to an extraordinary degree, Laurence. All the same, she gave her word, and I shall ensure she adheres to her word!”
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0012 }

Harriet’s expression appeared nearly unattractive due to its dark determination. On the upper floor, Clementine wept into her pillow.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0013 }

Thus Mr. Ashdown discovered his lady by herself and appearing extremely gorgeous. Clementine had not prepared any particular attire for the meeting; she wished to, yet she considered it ridiculous to adorn oneself for a gentleman whom you intended to reject. Consequently she was clad in her simple dark afternoon gown and possessed the appearance of a queen in it. The excitement she kept hidden tinted her countenance to a radiant glow, while her enormous blue eyes formed basins of illumination that were less calm than ordinary.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0014 }

She longed for the meeting to come to an end. All day long she had anticipated it with fear. She was entirely confident that John Ashdown held her in high regard in his own way—and she was equally convinced that he lacked the feeling for her that he had possessed for his initial love. She sensed that her rejection would cause him significant disappointment, though she doubted it would completely destroy him. Still, she detested delivering the rejection; she detested it for his sake and—Clementine admitted this candidly to herself—for her own. She was aware that she was capable of loving John Ashdown if—if she were allowed to do so. She was aware that her existence would become empty if, once turned down as a suitor, he declined to remain her friend. She was aware that she could find great joy with him and that she possessed the ability to bring him joy. However, blocking her path to joy was the immovable barrier formed by the vow she had given Harriet long in the past. Clementine had no recollection of her father. His death had occurred when her age was merely three. Harriet, being thirteen at the time, retained a memory of him, though without any particular affection. He had been a severe, aloof individual much senior to his attractive, comely spouse. Five years afterwards, their twelve-year-old brother passed away as well; following his passing, the pair of girls had continually resided solely alongside their mother. They had refrained from participating very openly in the societal activities of the Glen or Kettlebridge, even if, whenever they attended, the humor and vigor of Harriet together with the gentleness and charm of Clementine rendered them desired visitors. Each of them had experienced what people termed “a disappointment” during their youth. The ocean had failed to return Clementine’s beloved; while Lionel Fairlie, at that time a striking, red-haired youthful colossus, renowned for reckless driving along with boisterous yet innocent misdeeds, had engaged in a dispute with Harriet and deserted her in a sudden bout of resentment.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0015 }

No shortage of suitors appeared for the positions of Martin and Lionel, yet not one appeared to gain approval from the Ainslie girls, as they gradually slipped out of their youth and status as belles with no apparent remorse. Their devotion belonged to their mother, an individual with a long-term illness. A small realm of domestic pursuits—comprising books, pets, and flowers—was shared by the three, leaving them joyful and satisfied.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0016 }

A profound sorrow came upon them when Mrs. Ainslie died on the day Clementine turned twenty-five. Their initial state was one of unbearable isolation. Harriet’s mourning and despondency persisted with particular intensity, as prolonged, somber reflections were interrupted solely by outbursts of violent, fierce tears. Clementine was informed by the aged Kettlebridge physician that he worried about lasting desolation or an even darker outcome.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0017 }

On one occasion, after Harriet had spent the entire day in silence and refused to consume any food, Clementine had dropped to her knees beside her sister.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0018 }

“Oh, Harriet, I am still here with you,” she pleaded. “Do I mean nothing to you? Our love for one another has always been so strong.”
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0019 }

“You will not belong to me forever,” Harriet had uttered, shattering her quietness with severe force. “After getting married, you will go away from me. Only I will remain, entirely by myself. It is impossible for me to endure that idea—simply impossible. Passing away would be my preference.”
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0020 }

“Never will I take a husband,” declared Clementine, “never, Harriet.”
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0021 }

Leaning toward her, Harriet peered intently into the eyes of Clementine.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0022 }

“Do you solemnly give me your promise on that?” she asked. “Swear it using mother’s Bible.”
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0023 }

Clementine agreed immediately, being perfectly happy to indulge Harriet. It made no difference to her. She was entirely aware that she would not ever wish to wed a soul. The depths of the ocean held her love, which had descended there alongside Martin Crawford; and lacking love, marriage to anyone was impossible for her. Consequently, she gave her word without hesitation, even if Harriet turned the affair into a somewhat terrifying ritual. In the empty room belonging to their mother, they held hands across the Bible, and each swore to the other a solemn oath that marriage was out of the question for them and that cohabitation would be their lifelong choice.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0024 }

Harriet’s health got better from that moment on. Before long, her usual cheerful composure returned. Clementine and she resided in the old home contentedly for a decade, unbothered by any idea of wedlock or matrimony. They felt the burden of their vow very little. Whenever an available man encountered them, Harriet made a point to recall their agreement to her sister, yet she had not experienced genuine anxiety until Clementine brought John Ashdown home that evening. Regarding Clementine, Harriet’s fixation on that pledge had continually served as a minor source of amusement for her—up to recently. Currently, it was a ruthless chain, chosen by herself yet impossible to break free from. On account of it, she had to look away from joy this evening.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0025 }

Indeed, the timid, gentle, youthful affection she had bestowed upon her boy-lover could never be offered to someone else. Nevertheless, she realized at present that the love she could bestow upon John Ashdown was richer and more mature. She recognized that he reached depths within her character that Martin had failed to reach—depths that, perchance, the seventeen-year-old girl had lacked. Yet she was required to dismiss him this evening—to dispatch him home to his solitary fireside, his vacant existence, and his agonizing troubles, all because she had sworn to Harriet, a decade earlier, upon their mother’s Bible, that she would refuse to ever wed.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0026 }

John Ashdown failed to seize his chance right away. Instead, he spent two full hours discussing topics that were far from romantic. He went so far as to bring up politics, despite knowing that Clementine was always bored by the subject. She started to believe that she was completely wrong, and all at once her anxieties and hopes appeared absurd to her. A sense of flatness and foolishness came over her. Her face lost its warmth and her eyes lost their shine. John Ashdown was not planning to ask for her hand in marriage at all.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0027 }

And then, all at once, he got up, walked to the other side of the room, and inquired it while standing beside her chair. The room had become dreadfully quiet. St. Laurence even stopped purring. Her own heart was heard beating by Clementine, who felt certain that John Ashdown had to hear it as well.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0028 }

Gentle yet decisive, her refusal ought to have been spoken right then. For days, she had held her stiff, apologetic little speech in reserve. Yet in that moment, its phrasing was entirely erased from her memory. A negative answer was required of her—and all at once, she discovered an inability to utter it. The word was simply unutterable. That she did not merely possess the capacity to love John Ashdown, but truly loved him already, was now clear to her. Rejecting him from her existence felt like pure torment.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0029 }

Compelled to speak, she raised her bent blonde head and falteringly requested that he grant her a short period to—to think it over.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0030 }

A small amount of astonishment touched John Ashdown. Although his vanity did not exceed what is permissible for any man, his expectation had been that Clementine Ainslie would give her consent. That she possessed feelings for him had seemed fairly certain to him. What then accounted for this uncertainty—this pausing? Having passed the age of a school girl, she was not one to be doubtful regarding her own inclinations. A nasty jolt of letdown and alarm registered within him. Nevertheless, showing his ever-present mild politeness, he agreed to what she asked and departed without delay.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0031 }

“In a handful of days, I shall inform you,” stated Clementine, her gaze directed downward and her cheeks flushed.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0032 }

As soon as the door closed behind his exit, she returned to the interior of the room, wringing her hands together.
{: #nw-v05-c21-p0033 }
